# An Investigation into the Celestial Coordinates and Stellar Positions of the Entire Sky

<note>original: "周天星位經緯宿度考" (Zhōutiān xīngwèi jīngwěi xiùdù kǎo). This title indicates a technical astronomical treatise. It focuses on the <term>Lunar Mansions</term> (the 28 sectors of the Chinese zodiac) and the precise measurements of stars using a coordinate system similar to modern longitude and latitude.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of a Chinese astronomical manuscript detailing the coordinates and positions of stars across the celestial sphere.</summary>

<keywords>Chinese astronomy, stellar positions, celestial coordinates, lunar mansions, longitude and latitude, 28 mansions</keywords>

# An Investigation into the Celestial Coordinates and Stellar Positions of the Entire Sky

## The Supreme Palace Enclosure: Map of the Seat of the Five Emperors

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese star chart depicting the "Seat of the Five Emperors" (五帝座) within the "Supreme Palace Enclosure" (太微垣). Five large circles are arranged in a cross pattern (top, bottom, left, right, and center). To the left of the left-most large circle, three smaller circles are arranged vertically. Text labels and astronomical data surround the diagram.</image-desc>

Central star of the **Seat of the Five Emperors** <note>original: "Wudizuo" (五帝座). In Western astronomy, these stars are part of the constellation Leo. They represent the five mythical emperors of the five directions.</note>

**Longitude:** 166 degrees <note>original: "Jingdu" (經度). Chinese astronomy used a system of celestial longitude measured in degrees, often starting from the winter solstice.</note>

**Venus** <note>original: "Jin" (金), the Metal Star.</note>
**Mercury** <note>original: "Shui" (水), the Water Star.</note>
**Saturn** <note>original: "Tu" (土), the Earth Star.</note>

->The Palace of the Snake<- <note>original: "Si Gong" (巳宮). This refers to the sixth position of the <term>Twelve Earthly Branches</term>, used here as a coordinate to divide the celestial circle into twelve "palaces" or zodiacal sectors.</note>

->Compiled and Edited by the Calf-Embracing Master<- <note>original: "Baoduzi" (抱犢子). This is a pseudonym for the author, likely indicating a Daoist or scholarly hermit lifestyle.</note>

<note>
The terms used here reflect a blend of traditional Chinese "Mansion" positions and Western-influenced coordinate systems:
- <term>Mansion Degree: 宿度 (Xudu). The position of a star within one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.</term>
- <term>The Wings: 翼宿 (Yixiu). The 27th Lunar Mansion, making up the "wings" of the Vermilion Bird of the South.</term>
- <term>Magnitude: 星體 (Xingti). Literally "star body," used here to denote the brightness or classification of the star.</term>
</note>

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 degree in the Horn <note>The Horn (Jiao) is the first of the twenty-eight Lunar Mansions, marking the beginning of the eastern quadrant of the sky.</note> | 5 degrees 46 minutes North of the Equator | 188 degrees 12 minutes | House of Chen <note>The House of Chen (Chengong) corresponds to the Dragon in the Chinese zodiac, roughly equivalent to the Western sign of Virgo.</note> | Third Magnitude | 15 degrees in the Chariot <note>The Chariot (Zhen) is the twenty-eighth and final Lunar Mansion.</note> | 37 minutes North of the Equator | 185 degrees 41 minutes |

<note>
The celestial coordinates provided here likely represent two different systems: the equatorial system (relative to the Earth's equator) and the ecliptic system (the path of the sun). This dual tracking allowed imperial astronomers to maintain highly accurate calendars and omen-tracking records. 

The "Subordinate Minister" (Delta Virginis) was envisioned as a high-ranking bureaucrat assisting the Celestial Emperor. Its brightness is listed as "Third Magnitude," meaning it is a prominent star easily visible to the naked eye under clear dark skies.
</note>

# The Supreme Palace Enclosure
## The Left Wall

->East<-

<note>The Left Wall of the Supreme Palace Enclosure consists of stars that represent high-ranking civilian and military officials. These officials were believed to guard the celestial emperor and manage the affairs of the state from the heavens.</note>

| Longitude | First Eastern General <note>Original: 東上將 (Dongshangjiang). Identified in modern astronomy as Gamma Virginis (Porrima), a binary star system.</note> | Star Magnitude | Mansion Degree | Latitude | Longitude | Second Eastern General <note>Original: 東次將 (Dongcijiang). Identified as Eta Virginis (Zaniah).</note> | Star Magnitude |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 192 degrees 49 minutes <gloss>House of Chen</gloss> <note>The House of Chen (Chengong) corresponds to the Dragon in the Chinese zodiac and the western sign of Virgo.</note> | <gloss>Wood</gloss><br><gloss>Earth</gloss> <note>These elements, Wood (Mu) and Earth (Tu), designate the star's astrological influence.</note> | Third Magnitude | 3 degrees in the Horn <note>The Horn (Jiao) is the first Lunar Mansion, marking the start of the Azure Dragon of the East.</note> | 12 degrees 59 minutes North of the Equator | 190 degrees 59 minutes <gloss>House of Chen</gloss> | <gloss>Wood</gloss><br><gloss>Earth</gloss> | Third Magnitude |

<note>
The "First Eastern General" and "Second Eastern General" are part of the protective "Wall" of the Supreme Palace. In the Chinese bureaucratic view of the stars, these were not merely points of light, but active participants in the celestial government. The precision of the coordinates—given in degrees and minutes—reflects the advanced state of imperial Chinese astronomy, which was essential for maintaining the calendar and interpreting celestial omens that might affect the Emperor's rule. Both stars are listed as "Third Magnitude," indicating they are moderately bright and easily visible to the naked eye under clear conditions.
</note>

| **Officer** | The bottommost star in the chain, representing a lower official. |
| **Right Law Administrator** | The primary star, positioned to the lower left of the chain. |

<note>Technical Vocabulary:

- **Chariot Mansion** <term>軫 zhěn</term>: The 28th and final Lunar Mansion of the Chinese zodiac, located in the modern constellation of Corvus, used here as a longitudinal reference point.
- **Stellar Magnitude** <term>星躰 xīngtǐ</term>: Literally "star body," this refers to the perceived brightness of the star. A "Fourth Class" star is visible to the naked eye but is considered moderately dim.
</note>

# Six Magnitudes of the Celestial Bodies

| Wing Mansion Degree | Latitude (North of Equator) | Longitude | Southern Minister | Stellar Magnitude | Wing Mansion Degree | Latitude (North of Equator) | Longitude |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 12th degree of the Wing | 15 degrees 19 minutes North | 164 degrees 6 minutes | <gloss>7</gloss><br/><gloss>Metal-Water</gloss><br/><gloss>Earth</gloss><br/><gloss>Palace of the Serpent</gloss> | Fifth Rank | 8th degree of the Wing | 22 degrees 13 minutes North | 160 degrees 28 minutes |

<note>original: 翼 (Yì). The "Wing" is the 27th Lunar Mansion in the Chinese system, corresponding to the constellation Crater and part of Hydra. It represents the wings of the Vermilion Bird of the South.</note>

<note>original: 赤北 (Chìběi). Literally "Red North." This refers to the distance north of the "Red Path" (the Celestial Equator). In modern terms, this is northern declination.</note>

<note>original: 相南 (Xiāngnán). Translated here as the "Southern Minister." In the Supreme Palace Enclosure—which represents the imperial court in the sky—the stars of the "Western Wall" are named after high-ranking officials. The "Southern Minister" (Xiang) is one of the primary advisory stars in this grouping.</note>

<note>original: 巳宮 (Sì Gōng). Translated as "Palace of the Serpent." The OCR noted "Jǐ" (己), but in astronomical charts of this period, this identifies the zodiacal division of the Serpent, one of the twelve branches corresponding to the south-southeast direction.</note>

<note>original: 金水 (Jīn Shuǐ) and 土 (Tǔ). These terms refer to the Five Elements (Metal, Water, and Earth). In this context, they denote the planetary "nature" or astrological influence assigned to the star, used by court astronomers to interpret celestial omens.</note>

<note>The "Fifth Rank" (五等, wǔ děng) refers to the star's brightness. The Chinese system of six ranks closely mirrors the Western system of stellar magnitudes, where a fifth-magnitude star is relatively faint but still visible to the naked eye under clear dark skies.</note>

# Diagram of the Eleven Stars of the Left Wall
<note>original: 左垣 (Zuǒ Yuán). The "Left Wall" (or Eastern Wall) of the Heavenly Market Enclosure. In traditional Chinese uranography, the stars of the two walls are named after ancient Chinese states and regions, representing the idea that the celestial market oversees the entire realm.</note>

->Magnitude: Third Class<-
<note>original: 三等 (Sānděng). This refers to the apparent brightness of the stars. In this system, "Third Class" stars are of moderate brightness, visible to the naked eye under normal conditions.</note>

<note>original: 箕四度 (Jī sì dù). This specifies the star's longitudinal position relative to the Winnowing Basket (Ji) lunar mansion, one of the twenty-eight stations the moon passes through.</note>

### Technical Terms

<term>Coiled Thong</term>
<note>original: "貫索" (Guan Suo). A circle of nine stars. While the table provides a single coordinate point (likely for the lead star or the center of the grouping), the diagram shows the distinctive ring shape that gives the asterism its name.</note>

<term>Tail Mansion</term>
<note>original: "尾宿" (Wei Xiu). One of the twenty-eight Lunar Mansions, representing the tail of the Azure Dragon of the East. A "Mansion Degree" (宿度) measures how far a star has progressed through that specific segment of the sky.</note>

### Technical Terms

<term>Room Mansion</term>

<term>Mao Palace</term>
<note>original: "卯宮" (Mao Gong). One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiacal circle. In astronomical systems influenced by Western Jesuit methods (like the *Lixiang Kaocheng*), the "Mao" division corresponds to the sign of Scorpio.</note>

<note>original: "星體" (Xingti, literally 'Stellar Body') and "二等" (Erdeng, 'Second Class'). This refers to the brightness of the star. "Second Magnitude" stars are bright but not the brightest in the sky.</note>

### Technical Terms

*   <term>Heavenly Discipline</term> (*Tianji*): An asterism located within the Heavenly Market Enclosure, representing the officials who maintain the rules and records of the market. It is mostly found in the modern constellation Hercules.
*   <term>Longitude</term> (*Jingdu*): The angular distance of a celestial body measured eastward along the ecliptic or equator.
*   <term>Latitude</term> (*Weidu*): The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.
*   <term>Lunar Mansion Degree</term> (*Sudu*): A measurement of a star's position relative to one of the twenty-eight "Lunar Mansions" or stations of the moon.
*   <term>Stellar Magnitude</term> (*Xingdeng*): A classification of the brightness of stars.
*   <term>Palace of the Tiger</term> (*Yin Gong*): A thirty-degree segment of the sky used in traditional Chinese calendrical and astronomical systems.
*   <term>Winnowing Basket</term> (*Ji*): One of the twenty-eight lunar mansions, used here as a reference point for longitudinal measurement.

<margin>The Horn Mansion</margin>

# Investigation into the Degrees and Coordinates of the Celestial Star Positions
<note>This title indicates a scholarly "investigation" (kao) into the precise longitudinal and latitudinal coordinates of the stars across the heavens.</note>

->The Horn Mansion<-
<note>original: 角宿 (Jiǎoxiù). The "Horn" represents the horns of the Azure Dragon, a massive constellation spanning the eastern sky.</note>

## Diagram of the Horn Mansion

<image-desc>An astronomical diagram of the Horn (Jue) lunar mansion, consisting of two stars represented by small circles connected by a vertical dashed line.</image-desc>

->Compiled by **Baoyuanzi**<-
<note>Baoyuanzi (抱元子), meaning "Master who Embraces the Primal," is a Daoist pseudonym used by the author to signify a return to original cosmic principles.</note>

The Horn Mansion — **Metal** and **Fire**; **Palace of Chen**
<note>These refer to the "Field Allotment" (fenye) system. "Metal and Fire" associate the mansion with the planets Venus and Mars, while the "Palace of Chen" corresponds to the Dragon sector of the Chinese zodiac (roughly equivalent to the Western sign of Virgo).</note>

### Vocabulary and Key Terms
*   **Great Mausoleum** (大陵): An asterism within the Stomach Mansion.
*   **Mansion Degree** (宿度): The longitudinal position of a star measured within the boundaries of one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.
*   **Magnitude/Star Track** (星躔): The brightness or specific path of a celestial body.
*   **Longitude and Latitude** (經度/緯度): The celestial coordinates used to pinpoint the star's location on the heavenly sphere.
*   **Stomach** (胃): The third mansion of the Western White Tiger, representing the granary or the "stomach" of the heavens.
*   **Palace of the Dog** (戌宮): The eleventh division of the Chinese zodiac, roughly corresponding to the sign of Aries in Western astrology during the period this manuscript was likely produced.
*   **Celestial Kingdom/Orchard** (天國/園): A group of stars representing the imperial garden.
*   **South of the Equator** (赤南): Literally "Red South," referring to a position south of the "Red Road" (the celestial equator).

<term>Metal and Earth (金土, Jīn Tǔ)</term>: Astrological associations linking the star's influence to the qualities of the planets Venus (Metal) and Saturn (Earth).

<term>The Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū Gōng)</term>: One of the twelve "palaces" or zodiacal signs. Astronomers used these to divide the ecliptic into equal 30-degree segments for tracking planetary and stellar movements.

### Astronomical Glossary

*   **Celestial Boat** (天船, Tiān Chuán): <term>Celestial Boat: An asterism in the constellation Perseus, envisioned as a ship sailing the Milky Way.</term>
*   **Longitude** (經度, Jīng Dù): <note>original: 經度. In this context, it refers to celestial longitude—the position of a star measured eastward along the ecliptic.</note>
*   **Latitude** (緯度, Wěi Dù): <note>original: 緯度. Specifically, celestial latitude, measuring how far north or south a star is from the ecliptic plane.</note>
*   **Mansion Degree** (宿度, Xiù Dù): <term>Mansion Degree: A coordinate system that measures a star's position relative to the starting point of one of the Twenty-Eight Mansions.</term>
*   **Stellar Magnitude** (星躔, Xīng Chán): <note>original: 星躔. Literally "the treading of the stars," here used to categorize the brightness or specific placement of the star.</note>
*   **Stomach Mansion** (胃, Wèi): <term>Stomach Mansion: The third mansion of the White Tiger, associated with the storage of grain and celestial energy.</term>
*   **Palace of the Rooster** (酉宮, Yǒu Gōng): <term>Palace of the Rooster: One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac (equating to the branch 'You'), used here to define a 30-degree segment of the sky roughly corresponding to parts of Aries and Taurus.</term>
*   **North of the Equator** (赤北, Chì Běi): <note>Refers to the star's declination or position north of the celestial equator (the "Red Road").</note>
*   **Fixed Star** (恆星, Héng Xīng): <term>Fixed Star: A celestial body that remains in a constant position relative to other stars, as opposed to the planets.</term>
*   **Thorough Investigation of Astronomical Phenomena** (曆象考成, Lìxiàng Kǎochéng): <term>Lixiàng Kǎochéng: A monumental astronomical work commissioned by the Kangxi Emperor and completed in 1723. It synthesized traditional Chinese observations with new geometric and calculation methods introduced by European Jesuit astronomers.</term>

### Explanatory Notes

*   **Celestial Boat** (天船, <note>Tiān Chuán</note>): This asterism is envisioned as a great ship sailing across the Milky Way. It is primarily located within the stars of Perseus.
*   **Net Mansion** (畢, <note>Bì</note>): The 19th of the 28 Lunar Mansions. In Western astronomy, it corresponds to the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus.
*   **Mansion Degree** (宿度, <note>Xiù dù</note>): A measurement of a star’s position relative to the starting point of one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.
*   **North of the Equator** (赤北, <note>Chì Běi</note>): Literally "North of the Red [Road]," where the "Red Road" is the traditional Chinese name for the celestial equator.
*   **Latitude and Longitude** (緯度/經度, <note>Wěidù/Jīngdù</note>): These terms refer to the celestial coordinates used to map the heavens, mirroring the way we map the Earth.

To the right of this cluster sits a single solid circle, followed by a final pair of hollow circles connected by an upward diagonal line.]

# An Investigation of Celestial Positions, Coordinates, and Mansion Degrees
<note>original: "Zhoutian Xingwei Jingwei Xiudu Kao." This title indicates a comprehensive study of the heavens. "Zhoutian" refers to the entire celestial sphere, "Jingwei" literally means the warp and woof of a fabric, serving here as a term for longitude and latitude (coordinates), and "Xiudu" refers to the specific degree-measurements within the lunar mansions.</note>

## The Star Mansion
<note>original: "Xingxiu." While the word "Xing" generally means "star" in Chinese, here it refers specifically to the twenty-fifth lunar mansion. It is the fourth mansion of the Vermilion Bird of the South and is traditionally associated with the neck or heart of the celestial bird.</note>

### Chart of the Star Mansion

<image-desc>A star chart depicting the "Star" (Xing) mansion. Seven circles representing stars are arranged in a vertical formation: a chain of four stars leads down into a diamond shape of four stars, with the lowest star of the chain serving as the top vertex of the diamond.</image-desc>

->Compiled and Edited by Baoyuanzi<-
<note>**Baoyuanzi** (The Master Who Embraces the Origin) is a pseudonym or Daoist sobriquet for the author. This style of naming was common among scholars who studied astronomy, as it suggested a deep connection with the fundamental principles of the universe.</note>

<note>
The **Star Mansion** (Xing) consists of seven stars. In ancient Chinese astrology, this mansion was thought to govern the internal affairs of the palace and was sometimes called the "Seven Stars." It is located in the modern constellation of Alphard (Alpha Hydrae) and the surrounding stars in Hydra.
</note>

# Star Catalog: The Yellow Emperor’s Chariot
<note>Original: "Xuanyuan." This asterism forms the "Sickle" of the modern constellation Leo. In Chinese tradition, these stars represent the body of a dragon or the chariot of the Yellow Emperor, the foundational figure of Chinese civilization.</note>

### Page 5 — Coordinate Tables for the Third and Fourth Stars

<note>
The "Stellar Path" (Original: "Xingchan") and "Longitude" (Original: "Jingdu") provide the star's position along the ecliptic. "North of the Equator" (Original: "Chibei," literally "Red North") refers to its declination above the celestial equator.
</note>

<note>
**Technical Terms:**
- **Fourth Magnitude** (Original: "Si Deng"): A measure of brightness. On this scale, higher numbers represent fainter stars.
- **Earth Phase** (Original: "Tu"): One of the Five Phases (Wu Xing). In an astronomical context, this often designates the star's astrological character or its classification within the cosmological system.
- **Palace of Leo** (Original: "Wu Gong"): Literally the "Palace of the Noon Branch." In the late imperial period, Chinese astronomers mapped the twelve branches of their zodiac to the twelve Western signs; "Wu" corresponds to Leo.
</note>

| Longitude | Latitude | Lunar Mansion Position | Stellar Rank | The Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan) | Longitude | Latitude | Lunar Mansion Position |

| 134 Degrees 23 Minutes | 35 Degrees 58 Minutes North of the Equator | 6th Degree of the <term>Star Mansion</term> | <term>Third Magnitude</term> | <term>Palace of Leo</term> | 137 Degrees | 33 Degrees 15 Minutes North of the Equator | 2nd Degree of the <term>Extended Net Mansion</term> |

<note>
**Technical Vocabulary & Explanations:**
- **Star Mansion** (Original: *Xing*): One of the 28 Lunar Mansions of the Chinese zodiac. It corresponds to the heart of the modern constellation Hydra, though stars from Leo (like those listed here) are often measured relative to it.
- **Extended Net Mansion** (Original: *Zhang*): The 26th Lunar Mansion. As the stars of the Yellow Emperor's Chariot arc across the sky, their coordinates transition from the "Star" mansion into the "Extended Net."
- **Stellar Rank** (Original: *Xingmai*, literally "Star Pulse"): Used here to denote the star's brightness or magnitude. <note>original: "三等" (Third Magnitude)</note> refers to a moderately bright star visible even with some light pollution.
- **Palace of Leo** (Original: *Wu Gong*): Literally the "Palace of the Noon Branch." In the astronomical systems introduced by European Jesuits in the 17th and 18th centuries, the Chinese "Noon" branch was equated with the Western zodiac sign of Leo.
- **North of the Equator** (Original: *Chibei*): Literally "Red North," referring to the "Red Road" (the Celestial Equator). This indicates the star's declination.
</note>

<note>
The coordinates provided—134 and 137 degrees of longitude—place these stars within the "Sickle" of Leo. Given the third-magnitude brightness and these positions, these entries likely represent the stars known in modern astronomy as Adhafera (Zeta Leonis) and Rasalas (Mu Leonis) or neighboring stars in the Imperial Chariot's curve.
</note>

### Technical Definitions

**Longitude** <note>original: "經度" (Jingdu). The star's position measured along the celestial equator.</note>

**Latitude** <note>original: "緯度" (Weidu). Specifically, the distance from the celestial equator; in this manuscript, it is noted as "South of the Equator" (Chinan).</note>

**Mansion Degree** <note>original: "宿度" (Xiudu). The position of the star within one of the <term>Twenty-Eight Mansions</term>, the traditional Chinese lunar zodiac system.</note>

**Stellar Body** <note>original: "星体" (Xingti). Here referring to the brightness or classification of the star.</note>

**Extended Net** <note>original: "張" (Zhang). The 26th Lunar Mansion, associated with the constellation Crater in Western astronomy. It traditionally represents the spread wings of the Vermilion Bird of the South.</note>

**South of the Equator** <note>original: "赤南" (Chinan). A measurement of declination indicating the star is located in the southern celestial hemisphere.</note>

**Sixth Magnitude** <note>original: "六等" (Liudeng). The dimmest category of stars visible to the naked eye under ideal conditions.</note>

<note>The following notes provide context for the technical terminology found in the catalog.</note>

**Water Level:** <gloss>Shuiwei</gloss>. An asterism located in the modern constellations of Gemini and Canis Minor.
**Palace of the Goat:** <gloss>Weigong</gloss>. A zodiacal sector used to categorize the sky's 360 degrees into twelve equal parts.
**Mansion Degree:** <gloss>Xudu</gloss>. The specific position of a star measured from the start of its respective Lunar Mansion.
**Latitude:** <gloss>Weidu</gloss>. Here specifically referring to declination (distance from the celestial equator).
**Longitude:** <gloss>Jingdu</gloss>. Here specifically referring to right ascension or a similar longitudinal measurement.
**Magnitude:** <gloss>Xingdeng</gloss>. The classification of a star's brightness.
**Willow:** <gloss>Liu</gloss>. The Lunar Mansion following the Mansion of the Well; these stars are recorded by their position relative to the Willow's starting point.
**North of the Equator:** <gloss>Chibei</gloss>. Literal translation: "Red [Equator] North."
**Well:** <gloss>Jing</gloss>. The 22nd Lunar Mansion, the broader category for this section of the manuscript.

- **Latitude** (緯度): Here, it specifically refers to "South of the Equator" (赤南), measuring the star's distance from the celestial equator.
- **Longitude** (經度): The horizontal position along the celestial sphere.

<note>The "Palace of the Dog" (戌宮, Xū Gōng) corresponds to the eleventh branch of the Chinese zodiac. In the coordinate system used here, it represents a specific 30-degree segment of the ecliptic. </note>

<note>The "Magnitude" (等, Děng) indicates brightness. Star Three is a "Fourth Magnitude" star, making it moderately visible, while Star Four is a "Sixth Magnitude" star, which is at the very limit of what the human eye can see without assistance.</note>

<note>Latitude is recorded as "North of the Equator" (赤北, Chì Běi), indicating the star's declination in relation to the celestial equator. The units used are "Degrees" (度, Dù) and "Minutes" (分, Fēn).</note>

<note>The "Mansion Degree" (宿度, Sù Dù) measures how far the star is into the specific "Legs" segment of the sky. Curiously, both Star Three and Star Four are listed at the 9th degree, suggesting they share a similar longitudinal alignment within this mansion.</note>

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度, Xiù dù)</term>: The longitudinal distance of a star measured from the first star (the determinant star) of its specific lunar mansion. Here, the third star is 15 degrees into the Legs (Kuí) Mansion.

<term>Star Magnitude (星体, Xīng tǐ)</term>: Literally "Star Body." Used here to describe the brightness of the star; "fourth magnitude" indicates a star visible to the naked eye but relatively faint.

<summary>This page provides technical coordinates and elemental data for the third and fourth stars of the Outer Screen asterism. It notes that both stars reside within the Palace of the Dog and continue the sequence within the Legs Mansion.</summary>

->**The Second and Third Stars of the Pigsty**<-

The records here provide the precise coordinates for the subsidiary stars of the **Celestial Pigsty** <note>original: 天溷 (Tiānhùn). An asterism in the modern constellation Cetus.</note>. These stars are significantly dimmer than the first, classified as **5th magnitude** <note>original: 五等 (wǔ děng)</note>, meaning they would require excellent viewing conditions to be seen.

The third star is specifically noted for its position **11 degrees and 56 minutes South of the Equator** <note>original: 赤南 (chì nán)</note>, marking its place in the deep southern sky relative to the central mansions.

<term>The Gatekeeper (閽, Hūn)</term>: An individual star in the Chinese celestial map, often identified as Phi Andromedae or a nearby star. Its name implies its duty is to guard the entrance to the "Flying Gallery" or the forbidden celestial palace.

<term>Magnitude (星等, Xīngděng)</term>: The measure of a star's brightness. A "Sixth Magnitude" star is at the very limit of human visibility under dark skies, while a "Fifth Magnitude" star is slightly brighter.

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度, Xiùdù)</term>: A coordinate system measuring a star's position within one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.

<term>Latitude (緯度, Wěidù)</term>: In this historical context, this refers to the angular distance measured from the North Pole (Polar Distance), noted as "Distance from North" (去北, Qùběi).

<term>Longitude (經度, Jīngdù)</term>: The angular distance along the ecliptic or equator.

<term>Legs Mansion (奎, Kuí)</term>: The 15th Lunar Mansion, part of the White Tiger of the West. It covers parts of the modern constellations Andromeda and Pisces.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宫, Xū Gōng)</term>: A division of the Chinese zodiac corresponding to the eleventh Earthly Branch, roughly equivalent to the sign of Aries in Western astrology.

<term>Sixth Star of the Gallery (道六, Dào Liù)</term>: The sixth star of the "Flying Gallery" (Gedao) asterism, which consists of six stars in Cassiopeia forming a stepped path or gallery for the Emperor.

<margin>Palace of the Dog</margin>
<note>original: 戌宮 (Xū gōng). The "Palace of the Dog" corresponds to the eleventh branch of the Chinese zodiac and represents a specific 30-degree segment of the sky, roughly equivalent to the sign of Aries in Western astrology.</note>

### Key Terms and Concepts

<term>Wang Liang (王良)</term>: Named after a legendary charioteer of the Spring and Autumn period. This asterism is central to the constellation we now know as Cassiopeia. Astronomers watched these stars closely; if they appeared to shift or change color, it was thought to portend issues with the state's carriages or the safety of the Emperor's travels.

<term>Longitude and Latitude (經緯度, Jīngwěidù)</term>: The coordinates provided here use the "Equator North" (赤北, Chìběi) system, measuring distance from the celestial equator rather than the ecliptic.

<term>Magnitude (星躔, Xīng chán)</term>: Literally "The Star's Tread." In this context, it refers to the brightness or "rank" (等, děng) of the star. A 4th-rank star is visible to the naked eye but is relatively faint compared to the primary stars of the constellation.

<term>Legs Mansion (奎, Kuí)</term>: One of the 28 Lunar Mansions, part of the White Tiger of the West. It is traditionally associated with the "legs" of a person or a leaping animal and is considered a patron of literature and culture.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū gōng)</term>: One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac. As the stars move across the sky, they are categorized by which "Palace" or solar station they occupy.

### Explanatory Notes on Celestial Terms

<term>Wang Liang IV & V (王良四, 王良五)</term>: These stars correspond to Schedar (Alpha Cassiopeiae) and Caph (Beta Cassiopeiae). In traditional Chinese cartography, Wang Liang was a famous charioteer, and these stars formed part of his celestial carriage.

<term>Whole / Earth (全 / 土, Quán / Tǔ)</term>: The "Whole" designation implies the star is a primary reference point in the catalog. "Earth" refers to the Five Elements (Wu Xing) system, where stars were assigned elemental properties (Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water) believed to influence their astrological portents.

<term>Legs Mansion (奎, Kuí)</term>: One of the Twenty-Eight Mansions of the Chinese zodiac. It marks the first mansion of the White Tiger of the West. In Western astronomy, it occupies parts of Andromeda and Pisces.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū gōng)</term>: This is the eleventh of the twelve "Palaces" or Earthly Branches used to divide the sky into 30-degree segments. It corresponds to the area of the sky associated with the sign of Aries in the Western zodiac.

<term>North of the Equator (赤北, Chìběi)</term>: Literally "Red North," referring to the distance north of the "Red Road" (the celestial equator). This shows the use of an equatorial coordinate system, which was a hallmark of traditional Chinese astronomy long before it became standard in the West.

### Technical Glossary

<term>The Flying Corridor (閣/閣道, Gé/Gédào)</term>: An asterism in the Legs Mansion. It represents a raised walkway or gallery, symbolizing the path the Emperor takes between the Forbidden City and his gardens.

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度, Xiùdù)</term>: The longitudinal position of a star measured from the start of its respective Lunar Mansion.

<term>Latitude (緯度, Wěidù)</term>: Also known as declination, the distance north or south of the celestial equator (indicated here as "North of the Equator" or <note>original: 赤北, chìběi</note>).

<term>Longitude (經度, Jīngdù)</term>: The position along the celestial equator, similar to Right Ascension.

<term>Legs Mansion (奎宿, Kuí Xiù)</term>: The 15th of the 28 lunar mansions, making up the first mansion of the White Tiger of the West. It is associated with the constellation Andromeda and parts of Pisces.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū Gōng)</term>: One of the twelve Chinese zodiacal divisions (Earthly Branches) used to divide the celestial equator, equivalent to the sign of Aries in Western astrology.

<term>Star Rank (星林, Xīnglín)</term>: Literally "Star Forest," here acting as a category for the magnitude or brightness of the star. **Sixth Rank** is the dimmest category usually recorded.

### Technical Glossary

<term>Legs Mansion (奎宿, Kuí Xiù)</term>: The 15th of the 28 lunar mansions, making up the "buttocks" or "legs" of the White Tiger of the West. It encompasses parts of the Andromeda and Pisces constellations.

<term>Wall Mansion (壁宿, Bì Xiù)</term>: The 14th of the 28 lunar mansions, representing a "northern wall" or a "library" of the Black Tortoise of the North. It corresponds to stars in Pegasus and Andromeda.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū Gōng)</term>: A division of the Chinese zodiacal sky that corresponds roughly to the Western sign of Aries.

<term>North of the Equator (赤北, chìběi)</term>: A coordinate system similar to modern declination, measuring the distance of a star north from the celestial equator.

<term>Star Rank (星躔, xīngchán)</term>: Literally "the path or residence of a star," used here to classify the magnitude or the brightness of the star. A "Sixth Rank" star is quite faint to the naked eye.

<term>West of the Path (道西, dàoxī)</term>: Indicates the position of the specific star (in this case, the 11th star listed in this sequence) relative to the main structure of the "Flying Corridor" asterism.

### Technical Glossary

<term>The Whip (策, Cè)</term>: A singular star located near the Flying Corridor asterism. It is traditionally seen as the whip of the celestial charioteer, symbolized by the star Gamma Cassiopeiae.

<term>North of the Equator (赤北, chìběi)</term>: Literally "Red North." In traditional Chinese astronomy, the "Red Path" (Chidào) is the equator. This coordinate measures the angular distance north of the celestial equator, equivalent to modern declination.

<term>Palace of the Dog (戌宮, Xū Gōng)</term>: The eleventh station of the Chinese zodiac, corresponding to the branch *Xu* (Dog). In a celestial coordinate context, it aligns roughly with the Western zodiac sign of Aries.

<term>Legs Mansion (奎宿, Kuí Xiù)</term>: One of the twenty-eight lunar mansions. It is the first mansion of the White Tiger of the West and is associated with the constellation Andromeda.

### Technical Glossary

<term>Legs Mansion (奎宿, Kuí Xiù)</term>: One of the twenty-eight lunar mansions of the traditional Chinese star map. It consists of sixteen stars in the modern constellations of Andromeda and Pisces and is considered the "storage" or "library" of the heavens.

<term>Star Magnitude (星躰, xīngtǐ)</term>: A classification of a star's brightness. The traditional Chinese system used ranks (等, děng) similar to the Western magnitude system to categorize stars from brightest to dimmest.

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度, xiùdù)</term>: A measurement of longitudinal position within the Chinese system of 28 Mansions. Unlike modern 360-degree longitude, this resets at the start of each mansion.

### Technical Glossary

<term>Star Positions (星位, xīngwèi)</term>: The specific location of a star within the traditional Chinese constellation system.

<term>Longitude and Latitude (經緯, jīngwěi)</term>: While the terms literally mean "warp and weft" of a fabric, in this context they refer to the celestial grid used to map stars.

<term>Mansion Degrees (宿度, xiùdù)</term>: The measurement of a star's position within one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions, used to track the movement of the moon and planets.

<term>Orion Mansion (參, Shēn)</term>: One of the most prominent mansions, corresponding to the belt and body of Orion; used here as a reference point for the Beak Mansion's coordinates.

<term>Fourth Magnitude (四等, sì děng)</term>: A classification of a star's brightness; "fourth magnitude" stars are visible to the naked eye but are relatively faint.

# Punishment
<note>original: 伐 (Fá). This asterism represents a military judge or the act of punishing rebels. In Western astronomy, these stars form the "Sword" of Orion, hanging below the three famous belt stars.</note>

## The Second Star
### Elements: Earth and Wood
<note>original: 土木 (Tǔ-Mù). In Chinese astrology, stars were often associated with the Five Elements. This star's influence is governed by the qualities of Earth (stability/center) and Wood (growth/expansion).</note>

| Mansion Degree | Latitude | Longitude | Magnitude and Zodiac | Mansion Degree | Latitude | Longitude |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10th Degree of Three Stars | 5 degrees 41 minutes South | 79 degrees 17 minutes | Magnitude: 5<br/>Monkey Palace | 10th Degree of Three Stars | 5 degrees 6 minutes South | 79 degrees 17 minutes |

<note>The table lists the coordinates for the star. "Mansion Degree" (宿度) refers to the position within the Three Stars Mansion (Shen). "Latitude" is labeled as "Red South" (赤南), meaning degrees south of the celestial equator. The "Monkey Palace" (申宮) is one of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac, roughly corresponding to the region containing parts of modern Gemini and Orion.</note>

<term>Mansion Degree (Xiùdù)</term> — A measurement of a star's position relative to the starting point of one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.

<term>Celestial Toilet (Tiāncì)</term> — <note>original: 天厠 (Tiāncì)</note> A group of four stars in the constellation Lepus. In traditional Chinese astrology, this asterism was surprisingly important; its clarity was thought to predict the health of the populace and the proper functioning of the empire’s logistics.

<term>Well Mansion (Jǐng Xiù)</term> — <note>original: 井宿 (Jǐng Xiù)</note> The 22nd of the 28 Lunar Mansions, associated with the constellation Gemini. It marks the transition in the catalog from the Three Stars (Orion) region into the neighboring section of the sky.

<term>Palace of the Monkey (Shēn Gōng)</term> — <note>original: 申宮 (Shēn Gōng)</note> A division of the Chinese zodiac corresponding to the 9th Terrestrial Branch. In western celestial terms, this coordinate roughly aligns with the later part of the sign of Gemini.

<term>Star Magnitude (Xīng tǐ)</term> — <note>original: 星躰 (Xīng tǐ, lit. "Star Body")</note> This column refers to the brightness or size of the star. A "3rd Magnitude" star is moderately bright, visible even in areas with slight light pollution.

<term>Water and Earth Natures (Shuǐ Tǔ)</term> — <note>original: 水 土 (Shuǐ Tǔ)</note> These are the elemental "tempers" or planetary associations assigned to the stars. In this system, stars were believed to radiate the specific energies of the Five Elements, influencing the fate of those born under them or the outcome of events.

<term>South of the Equator (Chì nán)</term> — <note>original: 赤南 (Chì nán)</note> A measurement of celestial latitude (declination) taken from the "Red Road" or celestial equator.

<term>Celestial Granary (Tiānlǐn)</term> — <note>original: 天廩</note> An asterism consisting of four stars in the constellation Taurus. <term>Well Mansion (Jǐng)</term> — <note>original: 井</note> One of the 28 Lunar Mansions. The "Mansion Degree" (宿度) tells us how far the star has moved into the sky-sector governed by the Well (associated with the constellation Gemini).

<term>Star Magnitude (Xīngtǐ)</term> — <note>original: 星体</note> Literally "Star Body." This indicates the perceived brightness of the star. A "3rd Magnitude" star is moderately bright, similar to the stars in the Big Dipper’s handle.

### Technical Glossary
<term>Celestial River (天河 - Tiānhé):</term> A poetic and technical name for the Milky Way. In this context, it refers to a specific celestial coordinate or "palace" sector associated with the galaxy's path.

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度 - Sùdù):</term> A measurement of a star's position relative to the starting point of its designated lunar mansion.
<term>Magnitude (等 - Děng):</term> A ranking of brightness where lower numbers indicate brighter stars; the 6th magnitude is the faintest rank cataloged by ancient astronomers.

### Technical Glossary
<term>Celestial Yin (天陰 - Tiānyīn):</term> A group of stars within the Net Mansion. In Chinese judicial astrology, it was sometimes associated with the "shade" or hidden forces, representing the Emperor's hunting attendants or silent officials.

<term>Metal (金 - Jīn):</term> One of the Five Elements, corresponding to the planet Venus. Its presence here indicates the planetary influence or "nature" ascribed to the primary star of this group.

<term>Palace of the Rooster (酉宮 - Yǒu Gōng):</term> One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac (Earthly Branches). The Rooster Palace corresponds to the west and the autumn season.

<term>Star Positions (星躔 - Xīngchán):</term> A classical term for the movement and specific locations of stars as they "tread" through the heavens.

<term>Latitude and Longitude (緯度, 經度 - Wěidù, Jīngdù):</term> While these terms are used in modern geography, in this historical astronomical context, they refer to the star's position relative to the celestial equator and the vernal equinox or mansion boundaries.

<term>Celestial Loftiness (Tiāngāo)</term>: An asterism located in the constellation Taurus. In traditional Chinese astronomy, it was seen as a high platform or observation post.
<term>Stellar Magnitude (Xīngděng)</term>: A measure of brightness. "Sixth Magnitude" stars are the faint limit of what the human eye can see without the aid of a telescope.
<term>Mansion Degree (Sùdù)</term>: The position of a celestial body within one of the twenty-eight "Lunar Mansions" (Sù), which are segments of the sky used as a coordinate system.
<term>Net Mansion (Bì)</term>: The 19th Lunar Mansion, symbolizing a hunting net, located within the modern constellation Taurus.
<term>Three Stars Mansion (Shēn)</term>: The 21st Lunar Mansion, named for the three prominent stars of Orion's Belt.
<term>North of the Equator (Chìběi)</term>: Literally "Red North," referring to the distance north of the celestial equator (the "Red Road").
<term>Central Palace (Zhōng Gōng)</term>: A term used here to categorize the star's regional placement within the traditional Chinese star map.

### Explanatory Notes on the Diagram

The diagram illustrates a specific sector of the northern sky associated with the **Three Stars Mansion** (Shēn). The **Saline Pool** is depicted as a triangular formation of three stars. Surrounding it are three distinct groups of **Pillars**, each composed of three stars. 

In the traditional Chinese celestial bureaucracy, if the **Five Chariots** represent the transport of the celestial emperors, the **Saline Pool** provides the water for the horses, and the **Pillars** represent the infrastructure—such as hitching posts or gate markers—that supports the celestial procession. 

<term>Saline Pool (Xiánchí)</term>: An asterism in Auriga associated with the sun's ritual bathing and the essence of water in the heavens.
<term>Pillar (Zhù)</term>: Three sets of stars (often categorized as Inner, Central, and Outer) that provide structural stability to the region of the Five Chariots.
<term>Seven (Qī)</term>: A numerical notation frequently found in historical star charts to denote degrees of distance or specific positions relative to the lunar mansions.

### Key Astronomical Vocabulary

The following terms are used to define the positions of the stars in the celestial hierarchy:

**Five Chariots** (Wǔchē)
<note>original: 五車</note>
A group of five bright stars in the modern constellation Auriga, representing the transport used by the Five Celestial Emperors.

**Longitude** (Jīngdù)
<note>original: 經度</note>
The angular distance of a celestial body measured eastward from a reference point.

**Latitude** (Wèidù)
<note>original: 緯度</note>
The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator (or ecliptic, depending on the specific system used).

**Mansion Position** (Xiùdù)
<note>original: 宿度</note>
The specific degree of a star’s location within one of the twenty-eight Lunar Mansions.

**Magnitude** (Xīngtǐ)
<note>original: 星體, literally "star body"</note>
The rank or size of a star, used here to denote its relative brightness or classification.

**Net Mansion** (Bì)
<note>original: 畢</note>
The 19th Lunar Mansion, which includes stars in the constellation Taurus. It is traditionally associated with hunting and rain.

**Palace of Gemini** (Shēn gōng)
<note>original: 申宮</note>
One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiacal circle, used for calculating the movement of the sun, moon, and planets.

**North of the Equator** (Chìběi)
<note>original: 赤北, literally "Red North"</note>
The coordinate position north of the "Red Road" (the traditional Chinese term for the celestial equator).

# Map of the Celestial Orchard

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese star chart depicting the "Tian Yuan" (Celestial Orchard) asterism. The diagram consists of thirteen circular dots representing stars, arranged in a winding, roughly horizontal path across the upper half of the framed area. Some dots are filled solid while others appear as outlines. The title "天園之圖" (Map of the Celestial Orchard) is written vertically on the right side. In the left margin, the character "畢" (Bì - the Net mansion) indicates the lunar mansion to which this asterism belongs.</image-desc>

### Technical Glossary

<term>The Five Chariots <note>original: 五車 (Wǔchē); a five-star asterism representing the chariots of the five celestial emperors. Most of these stars reside in the modern constellation Auriga.</note></term>

<term>Longitude and Latitude <note>original: 經度 (Jīngdù) and 緯度 (Wěidù); used here in two different systems: the "Yellow Path" (Ecliptic) system and the "Red Path" (Equatorial) system.</note></term>

<term>Well Mansion <note>original: 井 (Jǐng); the 22nd Lunar Mansion, located in the modern constellation Gemini. It is often associated with water and order.</note></term>

<term>Net Mansion <note>original: 畢 (Bì); the 19th Lunar Mansion, corresponding to the Hyades star cluster in Taurus. It traditionally symbolizes hunting or social harmony.</note></term>

<term>Palace of Gemini <note>original: 申宮 (Shēn Gōng); the Chinese zodiacal equivalent to Gemini in the Western system, used to divide the Ecliptic into twelve equal parts.</note></term>

<term>North of the Ecliptic / Equator <note>original: 黃北 (Huáng Běi) / 赤北 (Chì Běi); "Yellow North" refers to measurements taken from the Sun's apparent path, while "Red North" refers to the Earth's projected equator.</note></term>

<term>Middle Palace <note>original: 中宫 (Zhōng Gōng); a classification used to denote stars located in the central sector of a specific zodiacal palace or celestial division.</note></term>

### Technical Glossary

<term>Star Magnitude <note>original: 星躔 (Xīngchán) or 五等 (Wǔ děng). Here, "Xīngchán" refers to the star's recorded position or movement, while "Wǔ děng" specifies it is a star of the fifth magnitude—relatively dim to the naked eye.</note></term>

<term>Net Mansion <note>original: 畢 (Bì). The 19th Lunar Mansion of the Chinese constellation system. It is associated with the Hyades star cluster in the modern constellation Taurus and was traditionally seen as a hunting net or a harbinger of rain.</note></term>

<term>Mansion Degree <note>original: 宿度 (Xiùdù). A measurement of a star's longitudinal position within one of the 28 Lunar Mansions, rather than a 360-degree absolute scale.</note></term>

<term>Longitude and Latitude <note>original: 經度 (Jīngdù) and 緯度 (Wěidù). These terms were standardized in Chinese astronomy through contact with Jesuit astronomers, allowing for precise mapping of the celestial sphere using degrees and minutes.</note></term>

### Technical Glossary

### Technical Terminology

<term>Longitude <note>original: 經度 (Jīngdù). The horizontal coordinate used to measure a star's position along the celestial sphere.</note></term>

<term>Latitude <note>original: 緯度 (Wěidù). The vertical coordinate. Here, it is specified as "Red North" (赤北), meaning the distance north of the Celestial Equator.</note></term>

<term>Three Stars Mansion <note>original: 參 (Shēn). One of the 28 Lunar Mansions, famously composed of the "belt" stars of Orion. It serves as a longitudinal marker for this part of the sky.</note></term>

<term>Mansion Degree <note>original: 宿度 (Xiùdù). This identifies how far a star has "traveled" into a specific Lunar Mansion, allowing astronomers to pin down its exact location.</note></term>

<term>Magnitude <note>original: 星等 (Xīngděng). A measure of the star's brightness; a 5th-magnitude star is relatively faint, usually visible only under clear, dark skies away from city lights.</note></term>

<note>
The presence of "Fourth Magnitude" (<term>四等</term>) and the use of 360-degree coordinates are hallmarks of the Qing Dynasty's astronomical synthesis. These records combined traditional Chinese lunar mansions (the 28 <term>Xiù</term>) with European geometric methods introduced by scholars like Ferdinand Verbiest and Adam Schall von Bell. The "Palace of the Tiger" indicates the star's position within the larger duodecimal division of the sky.

<note>The vocabulary section below clarifies technical terms used in the manuscript's data columns.</note>

**Technical Vocabulary**

*   **Tail Mansion (Wei):** The sixth of the seven mansions of the Azure Dragon of the East.
*   **Star's Tread (Xingchan):** A term used to describe the star's rank or its path across the heavens; in this context, it categorizes the star by brightness (magnitude).
*   **Mansion Degree (Xiudu):** A measurement used to pinpoint a star's location within its specific lunar mansion segment of the sky.
*   **Latitude (Weidu) and Longitude (Jingdu):** The coordinate system used to map the celestial sphere, often following the ecliptic or equatorial systems introduced to the Imperial Court.
*   **Palace of the Tiger (Yin Gong):** One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac, roughly equivalent to the area of the sky occupied by the Western sign of Sagittarius.
*   **Water and Fire (Shuihuo):** Traditional elemental classifications used to interpret the astrological influence or "nature" of the star.

<note>The coordinates provided here use the "Red Road" or celestial equator as a baseline. The "Mansion Degree" (Xiù dù) indicates the star's position relative to the Southern Dipper (Dǒu) mansion, which serves as a neighboring celestial landmark.</note>

**Vocabulary and Terminology**

*   <term>Winnowing Basket</term> (Jī): The seventh and final lunar mansion of the Azure Dragon of the East.
*   <term>Star 2</term> (Xiù èr): Specifically refers to Delta Sagittarii, the second principal star of this constellation.
*   <term>Longitude</term> (Jīngdù) and <term>Latitude</term> (Wěidù): The celestial coordinates used to fix a star's position on the heavenly sphere.
*   <term>Mansion Degree</term> (Xiù dù): A measurement of the longitudinal distance a star occupies within the specific span of a lunar mansion.
*   <term>Star Magnitude</term> (Xīng tǐ): Literally "star body," referring here to the brightness or "rank" of the star; a 3rd rank star is moderately bright to the naked eye.
*   <term>South of the Equator</term> (Chì nán): Literally "Red South," referring to positions south of the celestial equator (the "Red Road").
*   <term>Dipper</term> (Dǒu): Refers to the Southern Dipper mansion, which immediately follows the Winnowing Basket in the celestial sequence.
*   <term>Mars and Jupiter</term> (Huǒ mù): Literally "Fire and Wood." In traditional astrology, stars were often assigned the elemental natures of specific planets to describe their influence.
*   <term>Chastity Palace</term> (Zhēn gōng): A specific division of the zodiac used in later astronomical systems, often associated with the sign of Sagittarius in translated Western-influenced Chinese texts.

### Technical Vocabulary Definitions:
- **Heavenly Abyss** (天淵): An asterism representing a deep celestial pool.
- **Longitude** (經度): The horizontal coordinate on the celestial sphere.
- **Latitude** (緯度): The vertical coordinate, measured here from the celestial equator.
- **Mansion Degree** (宿度): The position of a star measured within the boundaries of one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
- **Star Magnitude** (星躰): Literally "Star Body," referring to the brightness classification of the star.
- **Dipper Mansion** (斗宿): A prominent star grouping in the southern sky.
- **Palace** (宫): A division of the ecliptic, similar to the Western signs of the Zodiac.
</note>

### River Drum III

<term>River Drum III</term>: The star Gamma Aquilae, part of the prominent trio in the constellation Aquila.
<term>Clepsydra Platform</term>: An asterism in Lyra near the star Vega, used for marking celestial positions.
<term>Stellar Magnitude</term>: A classification of a star's brightness; lower numbers typically represent brighter stars.
<term>Mansion Degree</term>: A coordinate system measuring a star's position relative to the starting point of one of the 28 lunar mansions.
<term>Longitude</term>: The horizontal coordinate of a star, measured here in degrees and minutes.

<term>Comet Path (Huidao)</term>: <note>original: 彗道 (huidao).</note> This term refers to the mapped trajectory or "road" of a comet. In historical Chinese astronomy, these tables were used to track the movement of "broom stars" (comets) against the backdrop of fixed stars to interpret their astrological omens.

<term>Celestial Body (Xingti)</term>: <note>original: 星躰 (xingti).</note> A general term for any distinct object in the sky, such as a star, planet, or a specific point on a comet's tail.

<term>Mansion Degree (Xudu)</term>: <note>original: 宿度 (xudu).</note> The position of an object within one of the 28 Lunar Mansions. This is similar to how we might say something is at a certain degree within a specific sign of the Zodiac.

<term>Ladle (Dou)</term>: <note>original: 斗 (dou).</note> Short for the "Southern Dipper" lunar mansion. Not to be confused with the Big Dipper, this is a group of six stars in the constellation Sagittarius that was vital for tracking celestial longitudes in the Southern sky.

<term>Latitude (Weidu)</term>: <note>original: 緯度 (weidu).</note> In this context, it refers to the distance north or south of the celestial equator.

<term>Longitude (Jingdu)</term>: <note>original: 經度 (jingdu).</note> The horizontal coordinate along the celestial sphere.

<term>North of the Equator (Chibei)</term>: <note>original: 赤北 (chibei).</note> Literally "Red North," referring to the "Red Road" (the celestial equator). This indicates the object is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.

<term>Imperial Chariot-way (Liandao)</term>: <note>original: 輦道 (liandao).</note> An asterism representing the private path or road for the Emperor’s carriage. In the sky, these stars are found in the modern constellations of Lyra and Cygnus, forming a "path" near the celestial Weaver Girl.

<term>Longitude (Jingdu)</term>: <note>original: 經度.</note> The horizontal position of a star on the celestial sphere.

<term>Latitude (Weidu)</term>: <note>original: 緯度.</note> The vertical position of a star; specifically, its distance from the celestial equator.

<term>North of the Equator (Chibei)</term>: <note>original: 赤北 (chibei).</note> Literally "Red North." Traditional Chinese astronomers referred to the celestial equator as the "Red Road" (Chidao), so this term indicates the star is located in the Northern Hemisphere of the sky.

<term>Mansion Degree (Xudu)</term>: <note>original: 宿度.</note> A measurement of a star's position relative to the starting point of one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.

<term>Ox (Niu)</term>: <note>original: 牛 (niu).</note> Short for the "Ox" lunar mansion (<note>original: 牛宿 (niuxiu)</note>). This is the second of the seven mansions of the Northern Black Tortoise, roughly corresponding to the modern constellation Capricornus. It was historically associated with agriculture and the draft animals used in imperial ritual.

<term>Magnitude (Xingdeng)</term>: <note>original: 星等.</note> A measure of the brightness of a star. In this specific entry, the value is left blank.

<term>Star Magnitude (Xingdeng)</term>: <note>original: 星等.</note> A classification of brightness. A "fourth magnitude" star is moderately dim, visible to the naked eye in clear, dark skies but not prominent.

# Study of the Degrees and Coordinates of Celestial Star Positions
<note>original: 周天星位經緯宿度考 (Zhoutian xingwei jingwei xiudu kao). This title indicates a formal astronomical treatise concerning the ecliptic longitude (經) and latitude (緯) of stars, as well as their specific positions within the 28 Lunar Mansions.</note>

## The Girl Mansion
<note>original: 女宿 (Nü Xiu). The Girl Lunar Mansion is the third mansion of the "Black Tortoise," the northern quadrant of the Chinese zodiac. In modern Western astronomy, these stars are found within the constellation Aquarius.</note>

## Diagram of the Girl Mansion

<image-desc>
An astronomical diagram depicting the "Nü" (Girl) lunar mansion. Four small circles representing stars are arranged in a staggered quadrilateral formation in the center of the frame. Labels in vertical Chinese script are positioned around the star pattern.
</image-desc>

Girl Mansion
One
<note>original: 一 (yi). This likely designates the primary or "determinative" star of the mansion, which is used as the reference point for measurements. In this case, it typically refers to the star Epsilon Aquarii.</note>

Water
<note>original: 水 (shui). This refers to the elemental association of the mansion. The Girl Mansion is traditionally linked to the element of Water.</note>

Earth
<note>original: 土 (tu). In this context, it refers to the "Earth Star," which is the traditional Chinese name for the planet Saturn, the planetary ruler associated with this mansion.</note>

Palace of the Rat
<note>original: 子宮 (Zigong). The "Zi" Palace is the first of the twelve Earthly Branches in the Chinese zodiac. In celestial terms, it corresponds to the region of the sky associated with the Western zodiac sign of Aquarius.</note>

->Compiled and Edited by the Master of Embracing the Origin<-
<note>original: 抱元子纂輯 (Baoyuanzi zuanji). "Bao Yuan Zi" is a Daoist-style pseudonym (literary name) for the author. "Embracing the Origin" is a common philosophical concept in Daoism referring to returning to a state of primordial unity.</note>

It includes a star map of the four-star quadrilateral and identifies its astrological associations with the element Water, the planet Saturn, and the zodiacal Palace of the Rat (Aquarius).</summary>

->**The Twelve Feudal Lords**<-
<note>This asterism represents a group of powerful states from China's Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods (approx. 770–221 BCE). In Chinese uranography, the sky was a mirror of the earthly imperial hierarchy. Curiously, while titled "Twelve Lords," this specific chart includes thirteen markers, adding the Moon among the earthly states.</note>

**The States of the West and Center:**
趙 (Zhao) — 魏 (Wei) — 韓 (Han) — 晉 (Jin)
秦 (Qin) — 周 (Zhou) — 燕 (Yan)

**The States of the East and South (including the Moon):**
月 (Moon) — 楚 (Chu) — 齊 (Qi)
越 (Yue) — 吳 (Wu) — 鄭 (Zheng)

<column-break/>

<note>The layout of these stars in the diagram reflects their traditional positions in the night sky within the Girl Mansion, serving as a celestial map for court astrologers to monitor the fates of the various regions of the empire.</note>

- **Latitude** <term>Weidu (緯度)</term>: Celestial latitude.
- **Mansion Degree** <term>Xiudu (宿度)</term>: The position of a star measured within one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.
- **Magnitude** <term>Xingti (星体)</term>: Literally "Stellar Body," here used to categorize brightness or magnitude.
- **Emptiness** <term>Xu (虚)</term>: The "Emptiness" Lunar Mansion, part of the Northern Black Tortoise quadrant.
</note>

The <term>Supporting Basket</term> asterism is located in the northern sky. In the tradition of the "Heavenly Officials," these stars were seen as the tools of the imperial silkworm rearing process. 

The technical data provided here uses several overlapping systems:
1. **Star Grade**: A measure of brightness (magnitude), where a "4th Grade" star is brighter than a "5th Grade" star.
2. **Palaces**: The <term>Ox Palace</term> and <term>Rat Palace</term> are part of the "Twelve Palaces" <note>original: 十二宮, shí èr gōng</note>, which are roughly equivalent to the Western Zodiac signs but calculated along the celestial equator.
3. **Mansion Degree**: This specifies the star's position within the <term>Dipper Mansion</term> <note>original: 斗宿, dǒu xiù</note>. This is not the Big Dipper, but rather the "Southern Dipper," which serves as the first mansion of the Northern Black Tortoise.
</note>

# Municipal Office
<note>original: 市府 (Shìfǔ). This asterism represents the administrative offices of the celestial market. In modern astronomy, these stars are typically found in the constellations of Serpens or Ophiuchus.</note>

<br/>

<term>Pure Water</term> <note>original: 全水 (Quán shuǐ)</note>
In Chinese astrology, stars were often assigned elemental properties. "Pure Water" suggests a star that exerts a strong influence over water-related phenomena, such as tides, rainfall, or the "yin" (cool/receptive) energy of the state.

<term>North of Equator</term> <note>original: 赤北 (Chìběi)</note>
Literally "Red North," this term describes the star's position relative to the "Red Path" (the celestial equator). A star listed as "Red North" is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.

<term>Palace of the Rat</term> <note>original: 子宮 (Zǐ gōng)</note>
The celestial sphere was divided into twelve "palaces" or "stations" (similar to the Western Zodiac). The Palace of the Rat corresponds to the northernmost position on the horizon and is associated with the mid-winter season.

<term>Mansion Degree</term> <note>original: 宿度 (Xiù dù)</note>
A measurement of the star's position within its specific Lunar Mansion (in this case, the Danger Mansion), functioning similarly to modern right ascension but measured in Chinese degrees.

# Diagram of Zaofu <note>Zaofu (造父) is an asterism named after a legendary royal charioteer from the Zhou Dynasty. In modern astronomy, these five stars are located within the constellation Cepheus.</note>

**The Ninth Star of the Heavenly Hook** <note>original: 天鉤九 (Tiāngōu jiǔ). This refers to the final star in the "Heavenly Hook" asterism, which curves through the constellations Cepheus and Draco.</note>
Longitude <note>original: 經度 (Jīngdù). This refers to the celestial coordinate measuring distance along the ecliptic or equator.</note>
Latitude <note>original: 緯度 (Wěidù). This refers to the celestial coordinate measuring distance north or south of the ecliptic or equator.</note>

### Explanatory Notes

In the traditional Chinese vision of the night sky, which mirrored the earthly imperial bureaucracy, these stars represented the workers responsible for maintaining the roofs of the celestial buildings.

<term>South of the Equator (赤南, Chìnán)</term>: Literally "South of the Red Road." The "Red Road" is the traditional Chinese term for the celestial equator. A measurement of 50 minutes indicates the star is located just slightly south of this central line.

### Explanatory Notes on the Celestial Treasury

The table above records the precise coordinates for the first two stars in the **Celestial Money** (<term>天錢, Tiānqián</term>) group. In the ancient Chinese view of the cosmos, the stars were not merely distant suns but representatives of terrestrial functions; this asterism served as the "treasury of the gods," symbolizing the wealth and currency of the celestial court.

<term>Sign of the Rat (子宫, Zǐgōng)</term>: This term refers to one of the twelve branches of the Chinese zodiac used to divide the celestial equator. While we might associate the "Rat" with a year of birth, in this context, it acts as a spatial marker for the section of the sky we now identify with Aquarius.

<term>Mansion Degree (宿度, Xiùdù)</term>: This measurement tells us that **Celestial Money I** is located **6 degrees** past the western boundary of the **Rooftop Mansion** (<term>危, Wēi</term>). These degrees were based on the time it took for the sun to move through the sky, roughly 365.25 degrees in a full circle.

<term>Magnitude (星等, Xīngděng)</term>: The star is classified as **4th Magnitude**. In this historical grading system, lower numbers represent brighter stars. A 4th-magnitude star is moderately faint, visible to the naked eye in the countryside but difficult to spot in modern city lights.

<term>South of the Equator (赤南, Chìnán)</term>: Literally translated as "South of the Red Road." The "Red Road" is the traditional Chinese name for the celestial equator. The coordinates for **Celestial Money II** show it sits significantly further south than the first star, placing it near the border of the modern constellation Piscis Austrinus.

**Translator’s Commentary:**

This page of the manuscript provides data for the continuation of the **Celestial Money** (<term>天錢, Tiānqián</term>) group. This asterism consists of ten stars located in the southern part of the Rooftop Mansion. Ancient astronomers viewed this cluster as the "money of the heavens," representing a celestial treasury or fund. 

The entry for **Celestial Money III** is particularly detailed. By listing its position within the **Sign of the Rat**, the text anchors the star within the <term>Twelve Earthly Branches</term> system used to divide the sky. The measurement of **Latitude** using the term "South of the Equator" (<term>赤南, Chìnán</term>) indicates that the observers were using a coordinate system based on the celestial equator (equatorial coordinates), which was a hallmark of traditional Chinese astronomy.

The final two columns indicate the beginning of the entry for the next star in the sequence (Celestial Money IV), noting that it shares a similar brightness and mansion degree with its predecessor.

# Unnamed Stars of the Rooftop Mansion

## West of the Roof <note>original: 蓋屋 (Gàiwū). An asterism representing a thatched roof or building, consisting of two stars in the modern constellation Aquarius.</note>

| Longitude | Latitude | Mansion Degree | Linear Difference | West of the Mansion | Longitude |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

Rooftop <note>original: 危 (Wēi). One of the twenty-eight lunar mansions, associated with the element of Water and the direction of North.</note>
<gloss>Water and Earth</gloss> <note>original: 水土 (Shuǐtǔ). This likely refers to the elemental characteristics assigned to this specific celestial region in traditional Chinese astrology.</note>
<gloss>Sign of the Rat</gloss> <note>original: 子宮 (Zǐgōng). A division of the Chinese zodiac equivalent to the modern Western sign of Aquarius and representing the cardinal direction of North.</note>

326 degrees 46 minutes

***

**Translator’s Commentary:**

This page marks a transition from named constellations to the classification of **Unnamed Stars** (<term>無名之星, Wúmíng zhī xīng</term>). In historical Chinese astronomy, stars that did not belong to a primary asterism but were bright enough to be recorded were documented based on their proximity to major groups—in this case, to the west of the **Roof** (<term>蓋屋, Gàiwū</term>) asterism.

The table headers indicate a highly sophisticated system of measurement. **Linear Difference** (<term>里差, Lǐchā</term>) often refers to corrections made for the observer's geographic location or a correction between different calendar systems. The coordinates provided for the **Rooftop** entry (326 degrees 46 minutes) place the observer's focus deep within the northern sky’s winter quadrant. The interlinear annotations (<gloss>glosses</gloss>) reinforce the integration of astronomy with the theory of the Five Elements (Water and Earth) and the Earthly Branches (the Sign of the Rat).

**Translator’s Commentary:**

The manuscript continues its rigorous charting of the heavens using the <term>赤道座標 (Chìdào zuòbiāo)</term> or equatorial coordinate system. The mention of the **Celestial Yard** (<term>車府, Chēfǔ</term>) is significant; this asterism was vital for imperial transport symbolism. The text also synthesizes astronomical data with astrological theory, as seen in the designation of **Venus and Mercury** (the elements of Metal and Water) situated within the **Sign of the Rat**. 

In the Ming and Qing dynasties, such records were not merely for navigation but were essential for the <term>欽天監 (Qīntiānjiān)</term> or Imperial Academy of Astronomy to maintain the harmony between the celestial movements and the earthly reign of the Emperor. The precise measurements—down to the minute—reflect the integration of traditional Chinese observations with increasingly sophisticated mathematical models, possibly influenced by European techniques introduced during the late 17th century.

## Diagram of the Encampment Mansion
<gloss>Encampment Mansion</gloss> <note>original: 室宿 (Shì Xiù). The 13th of the 28 Lunar Mansions, representing the "inner room" or the walls of the celestial palace. It corresponds to stars in the modern constellation Pegasus.</note>

### Encampment I
<gloss>Fire</gloss> <note>original: 火 (Huǒ). Likely referring to the planet Mars or the elemental association of the star.</note>

**Longitude** <note>original: 經度 (Jīngdù). In this historical context, this refers to the celestial longitude measured along the ecliptic or equator.</note>

341 Degrees 34 Minutes

***

**Translator’s Commentary:**

This section introduces the **Encampment Mansion** (<term>室宿, Shì Xiù</term>), which traditionally symbolizes the building of imperial palaces and administrative halls. The star listed as **Encampment I** (<term>室宿一, Shì Xiù Yī</term>) is identified in modern astronomy as Markab (Alpha Pegasi), one of the four stars forming the Great Square of Pegasus. The inclusion of <term>經度 (Jīngdù)</term> or **Longitude** reflects the sophisticated <term>周天 (Zhōutiān)</term> or "Celestial Circuit" system, which divided the sky into 365.25 degrees to match the days of the year, though later manuscripts often adopted the 360-degree system from European influence. The dual glossing of "Fire" and "Water" suggests a complex astrological synthesis, possibly weighing the influence of the star's planetary ruler against its seasonal position.

### Astronomical Terminology

*   **The Rampart (Lěibì)**: This group of stars was envisioned as a protective wall for the celestial military encampment. It stretches across several modern constellations, including Aquarius and Pisces.
*   **Wall Mansion (Bì)**: One of the "Northern Black Tortoise" mansions. It traditionally represents a library or a screen, but here serves as the reference point for calculating the longitudinal position of the stars.
*   **Palace of the Pig (Hài gōng)**: In the Chinese system of "Twelve Branches," this corresponds to the Western zodiac sign of Pisces.
*   **Magnitude (Xīngděng)**: The observers used a numerical scale to rank brightness; a "4th Grade" star is moderately faint, visible to the naked eye in clear, dark conditions.
*   **Mansion Degree (Xiùdù)**: A unique Chinese coordinate system that measures how far a star has progressed into one of the 28 segments (mansions) of the sky.

### Astronomical Vocabulary

*   **Longitude (Jīngdù)**: The horizontal coordinate used to specify the position of a star on the celestial sphere.
*   **Latitude (Wèidù)**: The vertical coordinate measuring the distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.
*   **Mansion Degree (Xiùdù)**: A system of measurement used in traditional Chinese astronomy to pinpoint a star's location relative to the 28 Lunar Mansions (equatorial segments of the sky).
*   **Magnitude (Xīngděng)**: The scale used to describe the brightness of a star as seen from Earth.
*   **Wall Mansion (Bì)**: A mansion consisting of two main stars that represent the wall of the celestial palace or library.
*   **Encampment Mansion (Shì)**: Represented by the "square" of Pegasus, this mansion was traditionally used to determine the proper time for building houses and temples.

### Vocabulary Review

*   **Imperial Guard (羽林軍)**: A large grouping of stars symbolizing a celestial army.
*   **Longitude (經度)**: The position of a star measured along the celestial equator.
*   **Latitude (緯度)**: The position of a star measured north or south of the celestial equator.
*   **Mansion Degree (宿度)**: A system of measurement determining where a star falls within the boundaries of one of the 28 Lunar Mansions.
*   **Magnitude (星解)**: The classification of a star's brightness; "6th Grade" refers to the faintest stars visible to the naked eye.
*   **Palace of the Boar (亥宮)**: A division of the Chinese zodiacal circle.
*   **South of the Equator (赤南)**: Literally "Equator South," indicating a negative declination.
*   **Encampment Mansion (室)**: One of the four mansions of the Northern Black Tortoise.

<term>左轄 (Zuǒxiá): The Left Linchpin. A star in the Chariot (Zhěn) mansion, traditionally seen as part of the axle assembly of the celestial chariot.</term>

<term>宿度 (Xiùdù): Mansion Degree. The position of a star relative to the boundary of its lunar mansion.</term>

<term>往度 (Wǎngdù): Outgoing Degrees/Longitude. The horizontal coordinate of the star on the celestial sphere.</term>

<term>巳宮 (Sìgōng): Si Palace. One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiacal circle, corresponding to the "Serpent" position.</term>

<term>星躰 (Xīngtǐ): Star Body. Here used to denote the magnitude or physical appearance/brightness of the star.</term>

<term>黃南 (Huángnán): South of the Ecliptic. Measurement in the ecliptic coordinate system, where the "Yellow Path" is the sun's apparent yearly track.</term>

<term>赤南 (Chìnán): South of the Equator. Measurement in the equatorial coordinate system, based on the "Red Path" or celestial equator.</term>

<term>長沙 (Chāngshā): Changsha. A star in the Chariot mansion (Zeta Corvi). In Chinese uranography, it is named after the prefecture of Changsha, symbolizing the importance of earthly administration reflected in the heavens.</term>

<term>星體 (Xīngtǐ): Star Magnitude. Literally "Stellar Body," here referring to the brightness classification of the star.</term>

<term>徑度 (Jìngdù): Celestial Longitude. The angular distance measured along the ecliptic or equator.</term>

<term>緯度 (Wèidù): Celestial Latitude. The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator (marked here as "Red South").</term>

<term>宿度 (Xiùdù): Mansion Degree. The specific position of a star within one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (Xiu).</term>

<term>軫 (Zhěn): The Chariot. The twenty-eighth and final lunar mansion of the Chinese constellation system, located in the southern sky.</term>

<term>辰宫 (Chéngōng): The Dragon Palace. One of the twelve stations of the Chinese zodiac, used to track the position of Jupiter and define celestial coordinates.</term>

<term>金土 (Jīntǔ): Metal and Earth. A classification based on the Five Phases (Wuxing) theory, used to determine the star's influence on terrestrial events.</term>

# Map of the Green Hill

<note>This diagram depicts the asterism "Green Hill" (Qingqiu), consisting of seven stars arranged in a circular loop. This formation is situated in the southern sky, associated with the constellation Hydra in modern astronomy.</note>

->The Palace of the Snake<-
<note>original: "巳宮" (Sìgōng). The sixth station of the Chinese zodiac, corresponding to the sign of the Snake and a specific sector of the celestial longitude.</note>

| First Star of Green Hill | Longitude | Latitude | Mansion Degree |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 7 Stars | 169 degrees 24 minutes | 29 degrees 50 minutes South of the Equator | 18 degrees into the Wings |

<term>青丘 (Qīngqiū): Green Hill.</term> An asterism of seven stars located south of the Wings mansion. In Chinese mythology, Qingqiu is a legendary land to the east inhabited by nine-tailed foxes; celestially, it represents a frontier territory or a forested hill.

<term>徑度 (Jìngdù): Longitude.</term> The angular distance measured along the celestial equator.

<term>緯度 (Wèidù): Latitude.</term> The angular distance north or south of the celestial equator. The text uses <note>赤南 (Chìnán)</note>, meaning "South of the Red [Equator]," to indicate its southern position.

<term>宿度 (Xiùdù): Mansion Degree.</term> The star's specific position within one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions.

<term>翼 (Yì): The Wings.</term> The twenty-seventh lunar mansion, representing the wings of the Vermilion Bird of the South.

<term>巳宮 (Sìgōng): The Palace of the Snake.</term> One of the twelve divisions of the Chinese zodiac (<note>the Twelve Earthly Branches</note>). Each palace corresponds to approximately 30 degrees of celestial longitude.

# Star Coordinates of the Green Hill (Continued)

| Star Name | Palace | Longitude | Latitude | Mansion Degree | Star Name | Palace | Longitude |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Second Star of Green Hill** | Palace of the Snake | 169 degrees 53 minutes | 33 degrees 15 minutes South of the Equator | 18 degrees into the Wings | **Third Star of Green Hill** | Palace of the Snake | 172 degrees 44 minutes |
| <note>Magnitude:</note> 4th Class | <note>original: 己宮</note> | | <note>original: 赤南</note> | <note>original: 翌十八度</note> | <note>Magnitude:</note> 4th Class | <note>original: 己宮</note> | |

<term>星躔 (Xīngchán): Star Coordinates/Celestial Position.</term> Literally "the path of the stars," this term refers to the recorded positions of celestial bodies.

<term>四等 (Sìděng): Fourth Class.</term> This refers to the stellar magnitude (brightness). In this system, stars are categorized by their visibility, with the first class being the brightest.

<term>己宮 (Jǐgōng): The Snake Palace.</term> Although the text uses the character <note>己 (Jǐ)</note>, this is a common clerical variant or error for <note>巳 (Sì)</note>, the sixth of the Twelve Earthly Branches, which corresponds to the "Palace of the Snake" in the Chinese zodiacal division of the sky.

<term>翌 (Yì): The Wings.</term> A shorthand or variant character for <note>翼 (Yì)</note>, the 27th lunar mansion. 

<term>赤南 (Chìnán): South of the Red Equator.</term> This indicates the star's declination is south of the celestial equator (the "Red Road" or <note>赤道 Chìdào</note> in traditional Chinese astronomy).

<note>The measurements provided—169 and 172 degrees of longitude—place these stars in the modern constellation of Hydra. The "Green Hill" asterism as a whole is thought to represent a mythical island or a forested hunting ground for the celestial court.</note>
